evidence.title: Optimizing deep learning-enhanced opportunistic osteoporosis screening from chest X-rays in Australia: Impact of follow-up and treatment adherence on clinical and economic outcomes
evidence.outcome: Clinical benefits from follow-up and adherence
evidence.effect: Optimizing follow-up and adherence could amplify clinical benefits by four- to five-fold.
evidence.quote: Optimizing follow-up and adherence could amplify clinical benefits by four- to five-fold.
evidence.sample_unit: simulated women aged ≥50 years undergoing chest radiography

evidence.title: Implementation of Digital Chest X-Ray with Computer-Aided Detection for Tuberculosis Screening Among Persons with Advanced HIV Disease in Maputo, Mozambique: A Retrospective Cohort Analysis
evidence.outcome: TB diagnosis rate among patients with normal CAD result (false reassurance from negative screens)
evidence.effect: TB was diagnosed in 30% (43/143) of patients with a normal CAD result, 52% (15/27) of abnormal non-suggestive, and 85% (58/68) of suggestive cases; NPV was 65.9%.
evidence.quote: TB diagnosis rates increased sharply with CAD score: 30% (43/143) in normal, 52% (15/27) in abnormal non-suggestive, and 85% (58/68) in suggestive cases.
evidence.sample_unit: patients with advanced HIV disease screened with dCXR/CAD

evidence.title: Clinical Characteristics of Gastrointestinal Malignancy and Validation of the IDIOM Model Among Patients With Iron Deficiency Anemia in Thailand
evidence.venue: JGH open : an open access journal of gastroenterology and hepatology
evidence.effect: Very-low-risk group still had 18.1% GI malignancy prevalence.
evidence.quote: However, even in the very low‐risk group, the prevalence of GI malignancy remained high at 18.1% (Table S3 ).

evidence.title: Optimizing Thyroid Nodule Management With Artificial Intelligence: Multicenter Retrospective Study on Reducing Unnecessary Fine Needle Aspirations
evidence.outcome: Malignant nodules misclassified as benign by AI (false-negative results)
evidence.effect: 123 malignant nodules (8.6% of malignant cases) were mistakenly identified as benign, mostly low or intermediate suspicion; authors advise active surveillance for all such nodules.
evidence.quote: However, 123 malignant nodules (8.6% of malignant cases) were mistakenly identified as benign, with the majority of these being of low or intermediate suspicion.

evidence.title: Evaluating algorithmic approaches to rare disease case-finding: a retrospective validation study using electronic health records
evidence.outcome: Negative likelihood ratio and sensitivity of rare disease case-finding algorithms
evidence.effect: Median sensitivity 3.8% (IQR 1.2–12.6%); median negative likelihood ratio 0.96 (IQR 0.87–0.99), so a negative result adds little information.
evidence.quote: Median positive likelihood ratio was 1167 (IQR: 125–4006), reflecting a strong signal for disease presence, and median negative likelihood ratio was 0.96 (IQR: 0.87–0.99), reflecting limited clinical utility of a negative result.
evidence.sample_unit: patients (research EHR cases and controls; 34 rare disease algorithms)

evidence.title: Invasive haemodynamic validation of an artificial intelligence echocardiographic tool for detecting heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
evidence.outcome: Negative predictive value and sensitivity of AI HFpEF detection versus invasive haemodynamics
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 30%, specificity 88%, PPV 86%, NPV 33% (exercise RHC, n=28); with PCWP/CO slope, sensitivity 27%, NPV 16%. Negative AI results cannot exclude HFpEF.
evidence.quote: Due to limited sensitivity, the tool is best utilized to enrich identification of patients with clearly abnormal haemodynamics rather than to exclude HFpEF, particularly in early or borderline cases.

evidence.title: Physician Consensus Stratification Reveals Performance Limits of Deep Learning for Smartphone-Based Pharyngitis Diagnosis
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity for bacterial pharyngitis across models
evidence.effect: All models had high specificity (96-98%) but low sensitivity (2-15%) for bacterial pharyngitis, so negative results miss most bacterial cases and physician review is needed.
evidence.quote: The high specificity (96–98%) suggests strong potential for reducing unnecessary antibiotic prescriptions through AI-assisted triage, while the low sensitivity (2–15%) necessitates physician review for suspected bacterial infections.

evidence.title: Diagnostic Performance of ChatGPT-4o in Detecting Hip Fractures on Pelvic X-rays
evidence.outcome: Missed hip fractures (false negatives) by ChatGPT-4o on pelvic X-rays, especially non-displaced fractures
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 78.0%, specificity 87.0%, NPV 79.8%; 22 false negatives, 68.2% of them non-displaced fractures
evidence.quote: Among 22 false-negative cases, 68.2% were non-displaced fractures, suggesting the model had greater difficulty identifying subtle radiographic findings.

commentary.bottom_line: One simulation of 10,000 women suggests that better follow-up of positive screens could raise clinical benefit four- to five-fold, but no study tests whether instructing users changes follow-up or reliance on negative results. Seven hazard studies show that negative AI results often miss disease, which supports the reason for the instruction without showing that it works.

perspectives.view: The only study linked to the practice models follow-up adherence among 10,000 simulated women aged 50 or older. It does not test user instruction. It reports that better adherence could increase benefit four- to five-fold. The simulated design, the indirect link to instruction, and a single study place certainty at very low.

Negative AI results missed disease across settings. TB was found in 30% (43/143) of patients with advanced HIV and a normal CAD result. AI HFpEF detection had an NPV of 33%, and pharyngitis models had 2-15% sensitivity. These studies document the hazard, and none tests whether instruction prevents it.

A low-risk label may still carry meaningful risk for the patient. In one study, 18.1% of a very-low-risk group had GI malignancy. In another, 8.6% of malignant thyroid nodules were called benign, and its authors advised surveillance. Patients told a result is negative may skip follow-up unless clinicians explain these limits.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions gives example labeling that pairs a positive output with an instruction to seek further clinical evaluation. The guidance is a draft and uses should language. The quoted text addresses positive outputs and does not specify how negative outputs should be framed for high-risk patients.

The simulation modeled older women in Australia and included no Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. The Mozambique study of patients with advanced HIV reported an NPV of 65.9%. This result suggests false reassurance may fall on populations with limited access to confirmatory testing.

commentary.research_gap: No study tests whether instructing users, through labeling, interface messages, or training, changes the rate of further evaluation after negative AI results in high-risk patients or the completion of follow-up after positive screens. Prospective deployment studies should measure follow-up completion, missed and delayed diagnoses, and whether the effect differs by the wording and placement of the instruction.
commentary.underserved_note: The single test of the practice was a simulation of older women in Australia and did not include Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One hazard study came from a low-resource HIV setting in Mozambique, but it measured missed disease rather than the effect of instruction. Health systems serving these populations have no evidence on whether instructions are understood or acted on by their clinicians and patients.
